o.A: These movements are expected effects of improved gastric motility.
o.B: They may represent tardive dyskinesia, which can be irreversible and is associated with cumulative exposure.
o.C: They are more consistent with opioid withdrawal than with metoclopramide toxicity.
o.D: They are benign age-related movements and do not require medication review.

o.A: Perform hand hygiene, use aseptic technique and recommended skin antisepsis, then apply a sterile dressing; clean or sterile gloves are acceptable.
o.B: Use sterile gloves, but omit skin antisepsis if the previous transparent dressing remained intact.
o.C: Use clean technique without aseptic precautions once a central catheter has remained complication-free for several days.
o.D: Use maximal sterile barriers with cap, gown, sterile gloves, and full-body drape because routine central-line dressing care should mirror insertion precautions.

o.A: Clean gloves, tap water for periurethral cleansing, and a reusable lubricant container.
o.B: Aseptic technique with sterile equipment, including sterile gloves, drape, sponges, appropriate solution, and single-use lubricant.
o.C: Sterile gloves with permission for the catheter to touch clean bed linen if resistance occurs.
o.D: Clean technique unless the client has recurrent urinary infection or major immunosuppression.

o.A: Keep the cart in service and document both findings for correction at the next routine inventory.
o.B: Remove the expired medication, but leave the low-charge defibrillator in service until scheduled maintenance.
o.C: Remove the expired drug and follow the backup/readiness process until the defibrillator is confirmed operational.
o.D: Leave both items in place if another emergency cart can be brought from a nearby unit when needed.

items.s: During a scheduled emergency-cart check, the nurse finds one expired medication and a defibrillator battery that is not adequately charged. What is the best action?
items.r: Expired medications should not remain available for patient use. Emergency carts and defibrillators require an organization-defined readiness and maintenance process, including battery charge. The cart should not be considered ready until the expired drug is removed and the defibrillator is restored or replaced according to that process.

o.A: Approach the fire even if smoke is starting to threaten the nurse’s evacuation path.
o.B: Aim at the top of the flames first, then pull the pin after the extinguisher begins discharging.
o.C: Continue fighting after the extinguisher is empty if the remaining flames appear smaller.
o.D: Maintain a safe exit path, choose the correct extinguisher, use PASS, and evacuate if safe control is doubtful.

o.A: Bed rails, bedside tables, call controls, doorknobs, commodes, and nearby equipment.
o.B: Ceiling tiles, upper wall corners, and light fixtures.
o.C: Prioritize floors and lower wall surfaces because they accumulate the greatest environmental bioburden during routine care.
o.D: Windows and ceiling vents unless blood or body fluid is visible.

o.A: Use the same CDC example sequence for all PPE ensembles and locations because sequence consistency is the main protection against self-contamination.
o.B: Use the approved doffing sequence, avoid contaminating skin or clothing, discard PPE appropriately, and perform hand hygiene.
o.C: Touch the front of the gown freely once gloves are removed because it is then considered clean.
o.D: Wear contaminated gown and gloves to the nurses’ station and remove them after documentation.

o.A: If source testing is negative, treat the injury as nonrecordable under OSHA Part 1904 because infection risk has been excluded.
o.B: Record sharps injuries on the OSHA log when they cause lost work time or restricted duty, rather than when exposure alone occurs.
o.C: For Part 1904-covered employers, record the contaminated needlestick and maintain required sharps information while protecting confidentiality.
o.D: Keep the event in employee-health records but omit it from OSHA logs unless an occupational infection is later diagnosed.

o.A: Use Standard Precautions when infection is known or suspected, then add Transmission-Based Precautions if the organism requires them.
o.B: Use Standard Precautions for tasks with anticipated blood or body-fluid exposure, but not for routine noninvasive bedside care.
o.C: Use Standard Precautions routinely in inpatient units, while outpatient settings rely mainly on diagnosis-specific precautions.
o.D: Use them for every client, selecting hand hygiene and task-based PPE according to anticipated exposure.

o.A: It turns current treatment preferences into actionable medical orders in addition to an advance directive; state availability varies.
o.B: It is mainly for healthy adults planning far ahead and replaces the advance directive once it is signed.
o.C: It records values for future discussion but does not function as a medical order during an emergency.
o.D: Use a standard POLST form across states because the resulting clinical orders remain portable once they are signed by the appropriate clinician.

items.s: A client with serious progressive illness already has an advance directive and asks how a POLST or similar portable medical-order form differs. Which explanation is most accurate?
items.r: NIH/NIA explains that POLST/MOLST forms provide guidance that healthcare professionals can act on immediately in an emergency and serve as medical orders in addition to an advance directive. They are generally used for people who are seriously ill or near the end of life, and patients should check their state because availability and form vary.
